item.title: 069: Expiations for Touching Untouchable Objects
item.description:
(Aspṛśya-sparśana-prāyaścitta-vidhiḥ)

Section 1: Liturgical Rules and Expiatory Rites for the Entry of Impure Persons, Animals, and Objects into the Temple and Sanctum, and Remedial Purification Rites

Sanskrit (Devanagari) & Transliteration (IAST)

अथ एकोनसप्ततितमः पटलः (अस्पृश्यस्पर्शन-प्रायश्चित्त-विधिः) atha ekonasaptatitamaḥ paṭalaḥ (aspṛśyasparśana-prāyaścitta-vidhiḥ)

अथास्पृश्य-स्पर्शने प्रायश्चित्त-विधिं वक्ष्ये — atha aspṛśya-sparśane prāyaścitta-vidhiṃ vakṣye —

(मूषकादि-स्पर्शनादौ प्रायश्चित्तम्) मूषक-सर्प-कृकलास-मण्डूक-मार्जार-नकुलादिषु गर्भागारं प्रविष्टेषु विण्मूत्र-विसर्जने च, तद् व्यपोह्य, पञ्चगव्यैः ‘आपो हि ष्ठा’ (मुद्रितपाठे आपो हिष्ठा) इति मन्त्रेण प्रोक्षयेत्। (mūṣakādi-sparśanādou prāyaścittam) mūṣaka-sarpa-kṛkalāsa-maṇḍūka-mārjāra-nakulādiṣu garbhāgāraṃ praviṣṭeṣu viṇmūtra-visarjane ca, tad vyapōhya, pañcagavyaiḥ ‘āpo hi ṣṭhā’ iti mantreṇa proṣayet.

item.title: 070: Bhaya-Rakṣārtha-Niṣkṛtiḥ
item.description:
(Remedies for Protection in Times of Fear/Distress)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 70th Chapter (Saptatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter outlines the specific ritual protocol to be followed when the movable deity icons (utsava-bera, kautuka-bera, etc.) must be concealed or buried in the earth (tirodhāna) to protect them from theft, desecration, or destruction due to threats like thieves (caura), enemies (śatru), or foreign invasion (paracakra-bhaya).

item.title: 071: Punar-Bālālaya-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules for Reconstruction/Re-establishment of the Temporary Shrine)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 71st Chapter (Ekasaptatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter outlines the rules for building and using a temporary shrine (bālālaya or taruṇālaya) when the main fixed deity icon (dhruva-bera) or the temple structure (vimāna) is damaged, decayed, or desecrated. It includes detailed architectural specifications for the temporary shrine, the zoning layout for placing the deities, fire offering protocols, the ritual transfer of the divine presence (śakti) into a water vessel (kumbha), and the subsequent installation inside the temporary shrine.

item.title: 072: Dhruva-bera-prāyaścitta-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules of Expiation/Repairs for the Fixed Deity Icon)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 72nd Chapter (Dvisaptatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter discusses the expiations, repair protocols (sandhāna), and replacement procedures for the main fixed deity icon (dhruva-bera) and temple structure (vimāna). It covers minor and major damages to stone and clay icons, the protective wooden cage (kāṣṭha-pañjara) used during renovations, the temporary projection of divine power (śakti) into a water vessel (kumbha) for short-term painting/repairs, and the procedure for rectifying damages in multi-deity installations (nava-mūrty-ādi).

item.title: 073: Kautukādi-jīrṇa-bera-parityāga-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules for Discarding Worn-out Movable Deity Icons)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 73rd Chapter (Trisaptatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter discusses the defects arising from worn-out, decayed, or damaged movable deity icons (jīrṇa-bera), the serious consequences of delaying their disposal, and the precise ritual procedures for discarding them in water or fire. It also provides an anatomical classification of the deity’s icon into four categories of limbs (mahāṅga, aṅga, pratyaṅga, upāṅga) and outlines specific expiatory and repair processes for each category of damage, concluding with rules for renovating painted icons.

item.title: 074: Ācārya-saṅkara-yogabhogādi-saṅkara-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules for the Mixing of Priests, Postures, and Icon Configurations)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 74th Chapter (Catuḥsaptatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter outlines the rules and expiations concerning the substitution or changing of priests (ācārya-saṅkara), the proxy rituals when a chosen priest becomes unavailable, the prohibition of altering the theological path of installation (e.g. from Yoga to Bhoga), the regulations for changing the posture (standing, seated, reclining) of deity icons, and the consequences of mixing retinue/incarnation icons (saṅkara).

item.title: 075: Utpāta-śānti-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules of Pacification for Portents and Bad Omens)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 75th Chapter (Pañcasaptatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter discusses the classification, effects, and pacification rituals (śānti) for various portents, natural anomalies, and bad omens (utpāta or adbhuta) that occur due to human sins or transgressions. It divides portents into three classes—celestial (divya), atmospheric (āntarikṣa), and terrestrial (bhauma)—and details specific rituals to rectify abnormalities in animate beings, temple structures, and deity icons, as well as portents affecting the royal household.

item.title: 076: Śānti-pañcaka-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules for the Five Kinds of Pacification)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 76th Chapter (Ṣaṭsaptatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter defines and outlines the procedures for the five-fold pacification system (śānti-pañcakam): Adbhuta-śānti (Pacification for Portents), Prabhūta-śānti (Abundant Pacification), Mahā-śānti (Great Pacification), Śuddhi (Purification), and Sarva-śānti (All-encompassing Pacification). It details the architectural construction of the sacrificial hall, the positioning of the fire pits (kunda), the ingredients for fire offerings, and special procedures for bringing rain during severe droughts (anāvṛṣṭi).

item.title: 077: Tantra-saṅkarādi-sarvadoṣa-prāyaścitta-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules of Expiation for Mixing Worship Systems and Unspecified Defects)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 77th Chapter (Saptasaptatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter outlines the expiations and purifications required when different systems of Vaishnava worship (tantra-saṅkara)—specifically the Vedic Vaikhānasa and the non-Vedic Pancharatra—are mixed, detailing the severe consequences of such combinations on the king and kingdom. It also defines general expiation protocols (sāmānya-prāyaścitta) for all unspecified ritual errors (anukta-doṣa) of minor or major severity.

item.title: 078: Pavitrāropaṇa-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules for Sacred Thread Offerings)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 78th Chapter (Aṣṭasaptatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter details the ritual procedures for pavitrāropaṇa (the offering of sacred threads) to the deity. It explains the purpose of the ritual, its timing, the preparation of the threads (lengths, knots, and materials), the purification and consecration on the eleventh day (ekādaśy-adhivāsana), the dedication of the threads on the twelfth day (dvādaśy-arpaṇa), and the concluding ceremonies.

item.title: 079: Mārgaśīrṣa-dvādaśī-samārādhana-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules for the Annual Expiation and Consecration on the Margashirsha Twelfth Day)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 79th Chapter (Ekonāśītitemaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter outlines the annual expiatory ritual (newnātirikta-prāyaścitta) performed to rectify any deficiencies or excesses in the daily temple worship accumulated throughout the year. The ritual is performed specifically on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, involving special fire offerings, bathing the deity with fourteen water pots, laying the deity on a bed of grass, reciting the four Vedas, presenting a golden sacred thread, and chanting prayers of apology.

item.title: 080: Agnikuṇḍādi-homopakaraṇa-devatā-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Deities of Fire Pits and Sacrificial Implements)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 80th Chapter (Aśītitemaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter details the esoteric associations of the fire pits (kuṇḍa), altars (sthaṇḍila), and various sacrificial utensils (spoons, pots, firewood, grass bundles) with their presiding deities. It also provides the detailed iconographical description for meditating on Agni within the fire pit, and defines the rules for offering oblations into the seven specific tongues (jihvā) of the fire, warning against the spiritual and physical hazards of making offerings in non-blazing parts of the fire.

item.title: 081: Yajñādīnāṃ Viṣṇupūjāṅgatva-Ūrdhvapuṇḍra-Pavitra-Snāna-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules for Daily Worship, Forehead Marks, Kusha Rings, and Consecratory Baths)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 81st Chapter (Ekāśītitemaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter covers essential foundational practices for daily Agamic worship. It outlines:

  1. The Agamic principle that all Vedic sacrifices and rituals are sub-limbs (aṅga) of Viṣṇu worship.
  2. The rules for wearing ūrdhvapuṇḍra (vertical forehead marks), detailing clay sources, colors, and symbolic shapes (e.g. lotus, fish, conch).
  3. The placement of the twelve sacred names (dvādaśa-nāma-nyāsa) on different body parts.
  4. The preparation, dimensions, and rules of purity for pavitra (the ring of kusha grass).
  5. The purification bath (brāhma-snāna) and the strict requirement to remember the seer (ṛṣi), meter (chandas), and deity (devatā) of every mantra to prevent the demons (asura) from stealing the ritual’s merit.

item.title: 082: Sandhyopāsana-mantra-ṛṣi-chandas-devatā-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules for Seers, Meters, and Deities of the Twilight Worship Mantras)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 82nd Chapter (Dvyāśītitemaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter details the specific seers (ṛṣi), meters (chandas), and presiding deities (devatā) for the core mantras utilized during the daily twilight prayers (sandhyopāsana / sandhyāvandana). It lists the assignments for mantras of water purification, the Gayatri, the Vyahritis, pranayama, the solar hymns (Mitra, Sūrya), and expiatory/cleansing prayers.

item.title: 083: Praṇava-svarūpa-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules on the Divine Form and Nature of the Pranava / Om)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 83rd Chapter (Tryaśītitemaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter presents the cosmic and phonetic analysis of Praṇava (Om). It explains:

  1. The Upanishadic declaration that “Om is Brahman”, analyzing the three letters A, U, and M, and matching them with the Vedas (Rig, Yajur, Sama, Atharva), Gunas (Sattva, Rajas, Tamas), and primary deities (Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Rudra).
  2. The cosmic anatomy of the Praṇava-puruṣa (the personified sound Om), correlating the physical and subtle components of the universe (underworlds, earth, stars, oceans, mountains, Vedas, and daily sacrifices) with the limbs and organs of the divine sound.
  3. The absolute necessity of prefixing all Vedic mantras and silent recitations (japa) with Om to prevent their spiritual efficacy from being lost.

item.title: 084: Sāvitrī-mantra-kalpa-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules on the Savitri / Gayatri Mantra)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 84th Chapter (Caturaśītitemaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter presents the comprehensive ritual science (kalpa) of the Sāvitrī (commonly known as the Gāyatrī) mantra. It details:

  1. The symbolic structure of the Gayatri as a cosmic goddess whose limbs and features represent the Vedas, Upanishads, fields of grammar, directions, and cosmic elements.
  2. The three-fold meditation (dhyāna) of the Sandhya goddesses across the three junctions of the day: Savitri (morning, swan-riding, Brahma-ruled), Gayatri (noon, bull-riding, Rudra-ruled), and Sarasvati (evening, Garuḍa-riding, Viṣṇu-ruled).
  3. The placement of the twenty-four syllables of the mantra on twenty-four specific spots on the human body (varṇa-nyāsa).
  4. The specific color, presiding deity, sin-cleansing power, and spiritual fruit (such as attaining specific worlds) for each of the twenty-four syllables.

item.title: 085: Tattvajñānopadeśa-Niṣkala-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules for the Instruction of Truth and the Unmanifest Form of Brahman)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 85th Chapter (Pañcāśītitemaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter introduces the science of metaphysical truth (tattvajñāna), responding to the request of the assembly of sages to Sage Marīci. It defines the word tattva (the essential nature of the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa) and describes the niṣkala (unmanifest, unattributed, and transcendent) aspect of the Supreme Brahman, drawing heavily on Vedic Upanishadic statements (such as ākaśāśarīraṃ brahma, aṇor aṇīyān, etc.) to depict His omnipresence and realization within the heart.

item.title: 086: Sakala-vidhiḥ / Bhagavato Jagatsṛṣṭi-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules for the Manifest Form and the Lord’s Creation of the Universe)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 86th Chapter (Ṣaḍaśītitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter outlines the transition of the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa from the unmanifest (niṣkala) to the manifest (sakala) state, using classical analogies such as fire emerging from wood through churning, and clay taking forms on a potter’s wheel. It describes the relationship between Viṣṇu (as the supreme agent), Śrī (as His eternal, all-pervading power of resolve, or Mūlaprakṛti), and the individual souls (jīvātman or kṣetrajña) who are bound by Prakriti and undergo cycles of rebirth due to beginningless ignorance (avidyā).

item.title: 087: Vaikuṇṭha-lakṣaṇam
item.description:
(Description of the Supreme Abode Vaikuntha)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 87th Chapter (Saptāśītitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter describes the supreme spiritual realm of the Vaishnavas (Vaiṣṇavāṇḍam), located above the golden cosmic egg (hiraṇmayamaṇḍam). It details the four distinct worlds of Viṣṇu (Āmōda, Pramōda, Sammōda, and Vaikuṇṭha) and their corresponding manifestations (Viṣṇu, Mahāviṣṇu, Sadāviṣṇu, and Nārāyaṇa). It further details the supremacy of Lord Nārāyaṇa, the creation of the cosmos by His free will (svalīlayā), and the birth of the four-faced creator Brahmā (Caturmukha) from the navel-lotus of Nārāyaṇa reclining upon Adisesha during the dissolution (pralaya).

item.title: 088: Dehotpatti-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules for the Manifestation and Origin of the Physical Body)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 88th Chapter (Aṣṭāśītitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter explains the physiological and biological process of the formation of the physical body (deha), from the digestion of food to embryological development. It details the three-fold classification of digested food (urine, feces, and semen/ovum), the conception process driven by the vital wind (vāyu) and divine destiny (daiva-yogena), the day-by-day and month-by-month development of the fetus in the womb, the seven bodily tissues (saptadhātu), and the biological factors determining the gender and features of the newborn.

item.title: 089: Bhūrādi-tattva-prakāśaḥ
item.description:
(The Exposition of Elements Beginning with Earth)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 89th Chapter (Ekōnanavatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter presents the classification of the human body and mind based on the five gross elements (mahābhūta), the ten senses (indriya), and the four inner instruments of mind (antaḥkaraṇa). It maps body parts and actions to their elemental origins, lists the characteristics of the three cosmic qualities (guṇa: Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas) and their corresponding spatial realms, and outlines the four states of consciousness (jāgrat, svapna, suṣupti, and turīya), culminating in the description of the embodied soul as a twenty-five-fold entity (pañcaviṃśaty-ātmakaḥ puruṣaḥ).

item.title: 090: Deha-lakṣaṇa-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules for Body Measurements and Inner Regions)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 90th Chapter (Navatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter outlines the subtle anatomy and inner spiritual geography of the human body (deha-lakṣaṇa). It details the dimensions of the body, the location and description of the internal fire-mandala (vahni-maṇḍala) with the deity Vaishvanara, the bulb of life energy (kanda) at the navel with the revolving soul (jīva), the dormant serpentine energy (kundalinī śakti), the solar-disk (arka-bimba) at the heart with Viṣṇu, the lunar-disk (candra-bimba) at the nose-tip with Nārāyaṇa, and the sixteen-petaled head-lotus (śiraḥ-padma) representing Vāsudeva.

item.title: 091: Hṛd-padma-madhya-bhagavad-dhyāna-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules for Meditating on the Lord in the Center of the Heart-Lotus)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 91st Chapter (Ekanavatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter explains the practice of meditating on the Supreme Soul (paramātmā), Viṣṇu, in the heart-lotus. It describes the physical-spiritual structure of the heart-lotus with its eight petals representing the aṣṭa-siddhis (eight spiritual powers) and its pericarp of Prakriti. It details how the lotus blossoms and turns upward through pranayama, revealing the inner fire, the golden flame (quoting the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad), and the four-armed deity Viṣṇu. It concludes by linking this inner meditation to the Vedic authority of Rigvedic hymns and the absolute necessity of daily worship (viṣṇv-arcana) for the twice-born (dvija).

item.title: 092: Nāḍī-cakra-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules on the Network of Subtle Channels)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 92nd Chapter (Dvinavatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter provides a detailed map of the subtle energy channels (nāḍī) in the human body. It begins by stating the traditional count of 72,000 channels originating from the root bulb (kanda) at the navel, and identifies the fourteen principal ones. It describes the path, characteristics, and elemental/cosmic associations of the three primary channels (iḍā, piṅgalā, and suṣumnā) and maps the remaining eleven channels (sarasvatī, varuṇī, pūṣā, hasti-jihvā, yaśasvinī, viśvōdarā, kuhū, śaṅkhinī, payasvinī, alambuṣā, and gāndhārī) to their specific terminations in the extremities (eyes, ears, tongue, hands, feet, and excretory organs). It concludes with a vivid metaphor comparing the network of minor channels to the veins of a pipal (aśvattha) leaf.

item.title: 093: Jīvōdbhava-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Exposition of Vital Winds, the Soul, and its Paths of Transmigration)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 93rd Chapter (Trinavatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter is a comprehensive Agamic exposition on the nature of the vital winds (vāyu), the embodied soul (jīva), and the post-mortem destinations based on karma. It begins by describing the ten vital winds (Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Udāna, Samāna, Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya), their colors, bodily locations, and physiological functions. It then defines the nature of the individual soul (jīvātman) and explains how it acts and moves after death through the processes of cosmic dissolution (pañcabhautika-pralaya). Finally, it describes the divergent post-mortem paths of the soul: the hellish realms (naraka) for the doers of bad deeds, the Path of the Ancestors (pitṛyāṇa / dhūmādi-mārga) for performes of ritual actions seeking temporary heaven, and the Path of the Gods (devayāna / arcirādi-mārga) for those who practice devotion and surrender to the Supreme Brahman, leading to final liberation in the realm of Viṣṇu.

item.title: 094: Saṃsāra-hētu-tattaraṇōpāya-mōxa-svarūpa-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(The Cause of Transmigration, the Means of Crossing It, and the Nature of Liberation)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 94th Chapter (Caturnavatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter outlines the core Vaikhānasa Agamic soteriology. It details the cause of worldly bondage (saṃsāra), describing how the embodied soul, deluded by the Lord’s māyā, becomes bound by passions and repeatedly cycles through births and deaths. It then presents the path to deliverance: seeking refuge in Nārāyaṇa, whose grace removes māyā and grants right knowledge (samyag-jñāna). Finally, it defines liberation (mōxa) and explains the four distinct states of release (caturvidha-mōxa): sālokya (residing in the Lord’s realm, Āmoda), sāmīpya (being near the Lord, Pramoda), sārūpya (having the Lord’s form, Sammoda), and sāyujya (absolute union with the Lord, Vaikuṇṭha), culminating in eternal service (nitya-kaiṅkarya) and merging into the Supreme Light (parañ-jyōtiḥ).

item.title: 095: Caturvidha-bhagavat-samāśrayaṇa-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(The Fourfold Seeking of Refuge in the Lord and the Five Forms)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 95th Chapter (Pañcanavatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter expounds the fourfold path of seeking refuge in the Lord (bhagavat-samāśrayaṇa): japa (recitation of mantras), huta (sacrificial offerings in the fire), arcana (image worship), and dhyāna (meditative union). It establishes arcana (worship of images) as the most effective path for all human goals. It then details the Vaikhānasa doctrine of the fivefold manifestation of Brahman (pañca-mūrti): Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, and Aniruddha. It maps these five forms to the five elements, the five sacred fires (pañcāgni), and the five vital winds, explaining their corresponding cosmic qualities (Dharma, Jñāna, Aiśvarya, and Vīrya/Vairāgya) and calling for their unified meditation through the eightfold yoga.

item.title: 096: Yama-niyama-āsana-prāṇāyāma-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules on Restraints, Observances, Postures, and Breath Control)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 96th Chapter (Ṣaṇṇavatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter expounds the first four limbs of the eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅga-yōga): yama (moral restraints), niyama (spiritual observances), āsana (postures), and prāṇāyāma (breath control). It defines Yoga as the union of the individual soul (jīvātman) and the Supreme Soul (paramātman). It lists the ten yamas and ten niyamas, outlines and classifies nine specific yogic postures (āsana), and provides step-by-step instructions on the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), including the classical ratio of 16:64:32 matras for inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (rēcaka), along with corresponding visualizations of the internal Fire, Sun, and Moon mandalas to perceive Nārāyaṇa in the heart.

item.title: 097: Pratyāhāra-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules on Sensory Withdrawal and the Eighteen Vital Points)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 97th Chapter (Saptanavatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter expounds pratyāhāra (sensory withdrawal), the fifth limb of the eightfold yoga. It defines pratyāhāra under five distinct types, focusing on the withdrawal of the senses from external objects, viewing all things as the Self, mentally relinquishing prescribed actions, raising and retaining the vital breath through the eighteen vital points (aṣṭādaśa-marmasthānāni), and locking the breath within the subtle channels. It lists the eighteen vital points of the human body, details their exact relative distances in angulas, and describes the method of drawing, retaining, and directing the vital wind through these points up to the eyebrow center to perceive the inner light.

item.title: 098: Dhāraṇā-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules on Concentration)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 98th Chapter (Aṣṭanavatitamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter expounds dhāraṇā (concentration), the sixth limb of the eightfold yoga. It defines dhāraṇā under eight specific forms: 1) stabilizing the mind in the Self, 2) concentration on the inner space of the heart, 3) concentration on the outer space, 4) concentration on Earth (pṛthivī) at the feet, 5) concentration on Water (ap) at the knees, 6) concentration on Fire (tējas) at the anus, 7) concentration on Wind (vāyu) at the heart, and 8) concentration on Space (ākāśa) at the eyebrows. It details the seed-syllables (bīja-mantra), boundaries, and corresponding forms of Viṣṇu (Aniruddha, Acyuta, Satya, Puruṣa, and Viṣṇu) for each elemental concentration, culminating in deep concentration on the supreme bliss-form (paramānanda-vigraha) of Nārāyaṇa.

item.title: 099: Dhyāna-bhēda-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules on the Classifications of Meditation)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 99th Chapter (Ēkōnaśatatamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This chapter expounds dhyāna (meditation), the seventh limb of the eightfold yoga. It defines dhyāna as the contemplation of the Supreme Soul (paramātman) by the individual soul (jīvātman), and divides it into two categories: unmanifest (niṣkala) and manifest (sakala). The unmanifest is further identified with attribute-free (nirguṇa) meditation, which contemplates the all-pervading, partless light of Nārāyaṇa residing in the heart-cave of all beings. The manifest (sakala) is identified with saguṇa (with attributes) meditation, which is divided into four techniques based on visualizing the elements (Earth/Mahendra, Water/Varuṇa) and cosmic disks (Fire/Sun/Moon) in the heart, where the deity is worshipped with attributes, ornaments, consorts, and retinue.

item.title: 100: Samādhi-vidhiḥ
item.description:
(Rules on Absolute Absorption and the Conclusion of the Text)

This document contains the Sanskrit text, IAST transliteration, and English translation of the 100th and final Chapter (Śatatamaḥ Paṭalaḥ) of the Vimānārcanākalpa (attributed to Sage Marīci, representing the Vaikhānasa school of Vaishnavism).

This final chapter serves as the grand climax and epilogue (granthōpasaṃhāra) of the entire Vimānārcanākalpa (also known as the Ayuta-grantha-saṃhitā). It expounds samādhi (absorption), the eighth and final limb of yoga, defining it as the equalized state of union between the individual soul (jīvātman) and the Supreme Soul (paramātman). It provides a detailed yogic methodology for consciously leaving the physical body at death (dēhatyāga-prakāra), raising the prana through the suṣumnā channel to exit via the brahmarandhra while chanting Om to merge into Vaikuntha. Finally, Sage Marīci concludes by declaring the lineage of this Jnanayoga (bequeathed by Brahmā) and asserting that since constant inner meditation is difficult, one must worship the five manifest forms (pañca-mūrti) of Viṣṇu on images (samūrtārcana) to attain the supreme state.
